s019.description:
Fake payment screenshot scam: how a "Payment successful" screen can show a green tick when no money was sent.
How shopkeepers get fooled by fake UPI/payment apps, and the one check that stops it.

Scammers use cloned payment apps (with a fake success sound), edited screenshots or fake bank SMS, and they strike when a shop is busy. On 18 Oct 2026 police in Moga, Punjab arrested two men accused of cheating shopkeepers this way; in 2021 a man in Delhi admitted fooling over 200 shopkeepers. The fix: before handing over goods, check the credit in your own bank or payment app, not the customer's screen.

Sources:
https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/punjab/moga-police-bust-fake-upi-payment-scam-arrest-2-for-cheating-shopkeepers
https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/delhi/man-arrested-for-cheating-over-200-shopkeepers-using-fake-payment-app-delhi-police-260411

s019.comment: Do you check every payment in your own app? 👇 Police say fake apps can even play the payment sound — only your bank app proves the money arrived.

s020.description:
Isaac Newton and the South Sea Bubble of 1720: how the genius behind gravity lost money in a stock bubble.
Why even smart investors buy at the top.

South Sea Company shares rose from about £130 in January 1720 to over £1,000 by June. Newton sold most of his shares early at a profit, then bought back in at roughly double the price before the crash. Estimates of his loss range from about £10,000 to over £20,000, and historians still debate the evidence. The famous line about calculating the stars but not the madness of people is attributed to him but not confirmed. Not financial advice.

Sources:
https://newtonandthemint.history.ox.ac.uk/global-financial-world/newton-and-the-south-sea-bubble

titles: Infinite Money at the Bottom of the Sea 🌊
s021.description:
Rai stones of Yap: the giant stone money that worked even after one sank to the bottom of the sea.
How stone money on Yap shows what money really is.

On the Pacific island of Yap, money took the form of rai — huge carved stone discs, the largest about 3.6 metres wide and around 4 tonnes. Most were quarried on Palau, roughly 400 km away, and brought back by sea. Big stones were rarely moved; ownership changed by everyone agreeing who owned them. One stone sank on the way home, and the islanders still treated it as existing and kept trading it. Today most of our money is also just numbers that everyone agrees on.

Sources:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rai_stones

#Shorts #history #money
s021.comment: Would you accept a sunken coin? 👇 On Yap, a rai stone that sank at sea was still traded — everyone agreed it existed.
